name: Masseter Botox

card.summary: Botulinum toxin injected into the jaw muscle to slim a wide lower face; reasonably studied for muscle prominence, but temporary, and a 2025 trial is the main data on bone effects.
card.note: Effects wear off and need repeat treatment; asymmetry and weaker chewing have been reported, and bone-density effects are still being studied.

quick.overview:
Masseter Botox is the injection of botulinum toxin type A into the masseter, the main chewing muscle at the angle of the jaw. The goal is to weaken the muscle so it shrinks over time, slimming a square or wide lower face. It is also used for teeth grinding and jaw pain.

Looksmaxxing forums discuss it both as a facial slimming option and as something that suits some skull shapes and not others. Several pharma-sponsored trials of onabotulinumtoxinA for masseter prominence have been registered, while use for appearance has been off-label.
quick.mechanism: Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at the nerve-muscle junction, which causes the injected muscle to weaken [18]. With less use, the masseter is reported to lose bulk over weeks [2].
quick.risks: Reviews describe adverse effects as minimal and short-lasting [2], while Wikipedia notes that injecting the masseter can reduce chewing ability and that spread of toxin can weaken unintended muscles [18]. Researchers have examined whether reduced chewing load changes jawbone density; one placebo-controlled trial found no clinically significant change [3], while a smaller retrospective radiograph study in bruxism patients found region-specific reductions in a bone texture measure [5].

lead: Masseter Botox is the injection of botulinum toxin type A into the masseter, the main chewing muscle at the angle of the jaw [17]. The appearance goal is to slim a wide, square or bulky lower face: when the muscle is weakened it shrinks with disuse, and the outline of the lower face narrows over a few weeks [2][21]. It is also used for teeth grinding (bruxism), clenching and jaw pain [2].

The research base is larger than for most cosmetic procedures discussed in appearance forums. Case series from Asia in the 2000s reported masseter thickness down roughly 30 percent by three months [21][22], reviews describe reduced muscle bulk with minimal and short-lived side effects [1][2], and company-sponsored randomised trials show larger reductions in lower-facial volume than placebo at day 90 [13][10]. Results last months, not years, so treatment is repeated if people want to keep the effect [1].

Questions that remain active include how toxin affects jaw bone over repeat treatments, how outcomes differ by face shape, and the lack of a standard protocol [1][3][5]. On looksmax.org the procedure is a staple of lower-third and hollow-cheek discussion [15][16].

chain: The muscle shrinks with disuse over weeks
The lower face looks narrower and more defined
angle.text: Weakening the masseter shrinks its bulk, so a wide or square lower face reads as slimmer and the area under the cheekbone can look more hollow. People also use it to ease clenching and jaw tension.

paras: The masseter is the thick, quadrilateral chewing muscle running from the cheekbone to the outer angle of the lower jaw. It has superficial, deep and coronoid portions, closes the jaw, and is supplied by the mandibular nerve [17]. In people who clench, grind their teeth or chew heavily, the muscle can enlarge, sometimes more on one side, which can widen the lower face and produce asymmetry [17][2]. Masseter hypertrophy, or masseter muscle prominence in the language of recent trials, is the clinical term for this enlargement.

Botulinum toxin type A works by cleaving SNAP-25, a protein nerve terminals need to release acetylcholine, so the injected muscle receives a weaker signal until the nerve terminal regenerates [18]. When the masseter is used less, it gradually loses bulk. Proponents and clinicians describe the visible result as a narrower, softer lower-face outline seen from the front, and in some people more definition under the cheekbone [2][21].

The main appearance use is slimming a wide or square lower face. A 2019 review in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery concluded that injection into the lower back portion of the masseter reduces muscle bulk and reshapes the lower face, and that it can be combined with other toxin treatments as part of full-face contouring [2]. A 2022 review of 40 articles, 14 of which had at least 10 participants, concluded the treatment is effective for lower-face contouring but noted that no standard guidelines exist and that the number of units and injection points varied widely between studies [1].

In a retrospective review of 80 patients at a dermatology clinic, 18 sought only contouring, 28 sought only bruxism relief and 34 sought both, which illustrates how the cosmetic and functional uses overlap in practice [20]. A 2021 review of cosmetic toxins in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery covers the masseter alongside the upper face and platysma [28].

Clinically, masseter injection is used for bruxism and masticatory (jaw) muscle pain, and reviews report improvements in grinding, clenching and pain alongside the cosmetic change [2]. A registered Phase 4 trial compared toxin with an occlusal splint for masseter pain [14]. Grokipedia describes dentists adopting the approach off-label around 2010 [19]; because that page is AI-generated and some of its citations do not match its claims, it is used here only for general context.

Cosmetic use of botulinum toxin began with Richard Clark's 1989 report of correcting forehead asymmetry, and the US FDA approved Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines in 2002 [18]. Reports of treating masseter hypertrophy with the toxin appeared in the 1990s, with Grokipedia dating the first reported aesthetic use for masseter hypertrophy to 1994 [19]. A 2001 prospective study of five patients with ultrasound and EMG found a maximal 31 percent reduction in muscle bulk three months after treatment, with the effect stable at one year in six of nine muscles and repeat injection needed in three [22].

Aesthetic contouring then grew in East Asia; Grokipedia describes particular popularity in South Korea among patients seeking a softer, oval jawline [19]. Park and colleagues (2003) followed 45 patients and measured masseter thickness by ultrasound and CT, reporting reduced thickness over three months [23]. Kim and colleagues (2005) reported a case series of 1,021 patients treated between 2001 and 2002, with masseter thickness down an average of 31 percent at three months in the 383 who were followed; they concluded that the toxin could replace surgical masseter resection [21].

The pharmaceutical industry later ran formal trials. AbbVie/Allergan conducted a Phase 2 study that began in 2014 and a Phase 2b study that began in 2019, followed by Phase 3 programmes starting in 2023 and 2024 [13][10][11][12][26][27]. Google Trends data show that search interest in masseter Botox fluctuated by more than 50 percent in single weeks, which the authors list among a handful of cosmetic terms with that volatility [4].

The best-documented measure comes from the Allergan-sponsored Phase 2 trial (NCT02010775), a randomised, double-masked study of 187 adults aged 18 to 50 with masseter hypertrophy. Four toxin dose levels and saline placebo were compared. Using 3D imaging, lower-face volume at day 90 fell by about 4.4 cm3 at the lowest dose and about 8.2 cm3 at the highest, compared with about 0.5 cm3 for placebo, and the share of participants with a prominence-scale grade of 3 or lower ranged from 67 to about 90 percent across doses against 35 percent for placebo [13].

The Phase 2b trial (NCT03861936) randomised 150 adults at 14 US sites to two toxin dose levels or placebo. At day 90, an investigator-rated grade of minimal to moderate prominence was reached by about 91 percent of each toxin group and 22 percent of the placebo group; about 66 to 72 percent of toxin-treated participants and 11 percent of placebo had an improvement of at least two grades; and lower-facial volume change was about -6 cm3 in toxin groups versus -0.3 cm3 for placebo [10]. Most participants were women with a mean age near 39 [10]. A Japanese Phase 3 trial of 259 adults, with a primary endpoint of at least a two-grade improvement at day 90, and further Phase 3 trials of about 200 to 250 participants were registered as completed by 2025; no results were posted on the Japanese record [11][12][26][27].

Earlier open-label studies found similar magnitudes. The 2001 ultrasound study and the 1,021-patient series both reported roughly 31 percent thinner muscle at three months [22][21]. The 2022 review states that maximum effect after one session usually appears around three months and may last six to twelve months, with repeat sessions needed for longer-term results [1]. Kim and colleagues also cautioned that, after the masseter shrinks, the cheekbone and jaw angle can look relatively more prominent, so facial anatomy needs careful assessment [21].

The 2019 review described adverse effects as minimal and short-lived [2]. In the Phase 2 trial the most common events were facial paresis (four people at the highest dose), mastication disorder, headache and ordinary infections, with no deaths; the few serious events listed across arms, placebo included, were such things as appendicitis, a kidney infection and a fall [13]. In the Phase 2b trial, muscular weakness appeared in three participants at the higher dose and none on placebo [10]. Park and colleagues reported chewing difficulty, muscle aching and speech disturbance that generally resolved within one to four weeks [23].

In the 80-patient dermatology review, 15 patients (18.8 percent) had 16 treatment-related side effects, including smile asymmetry and paradoxical bulging in two patients each; the authors still describe the treatment as minimally invasive and effective while noting that significant side effects remain possible [20]. Wikipedia's botulinum toxin article states that masseter injection can reduce the ability to chew solid food and that toxin can spread to unintended muscles; it also lists headache, flu-like symptoms and allergic reactions as cosmetic-use effects [18]. Grokipedia lists contraindications such as pregnancy, breastfeeding, neuromuscular disease and active infection [19]. In 2009 the FDA added boxed warnings about distant spread of toxin to botulinum toxin products [18].

Because the masseter loads the mandible, researchers have asked whether prolonged weakening could thin the bone. In adult rabbits, a single toxin injection reduced bite force and was followed by lower bone quantity and quality at underloaded sites of the jaw at four weeks, with the condylar head still showing low bone area at twelve weeks [24]. In humans, a prespecified CT subpopulation of 123 people from the 12-month, placebo-controlled study found no clinically significant change in mandibular bone density in the condyle, premolar area or ramus after one or two treatments [3], and a follow-up CT analysis of bone morphology has been published [8]. A retrospective study of 42 bruxism patients found statistically significant reductions in a fractal-dimension bone-texture measure in the angle region, without a significant difference from controls after treatment [5]. A porcine study examined histology and myosin changes in the treated muscle [7].

In the US, Botox is approved for several indications, and masseter reduction for appearance has been off-label; company-sponsored Phase 2 and 3 programmes have since been run for masseter muscle prominence [19][10][11]. Grokipedia states that in the UK the toxin is a prescription-only medicine and that, in the US, insurance may cover TMJ-related use while cosmetic slimming is typically paid out of pocket [19]. Wikipedia lists the cosmetic toxins in circulation, including Botox/Vistabel, Dysport/Azzalure, Xeomin/Bocouture and Jeuveau/Nuceiva [18].

Descriptions of the procedure in general terms say a trained provider has the patient clench to locate the muscle, avoids the nerve and the smile muscles, injects at several points per side, and that effects begin over two to four weeks and last for several months [19]. Providers' protocols and units differ, and no standard guideline exists [1].

Human research on masseter toxin includes a 2001 five-patient ultrasound/EMG study, a 2003 45-patient prospective study and a 2005 1,021-patient case series of the Dysport formulation, all describing a muscle-thickness reduction of roughly 30 percent by three months [22][23][21]. Randomised, placebo-controlled trials of onabotulinumtoxinA for masseter prominence (Phase 2 n=187, Phase 2b n=150) reported significant improvement over placebo at day 90 [13][10]. Phase 3 trials in Japan and elsewhere completed in 2025 [11][12][26][27]. Imaging studies have examined bone density and morphology [3][8][5]. A study of Instagram posts tagged masseter Botox rated the reliability of video information as very low, and a review of internet material on masseter Botox for bruxism assessed information quality [6][9].

On looksmax.org, masseter Botox is discussed as a way to slim the lower third, produce hollows under the cheekbones and relieve jaw tension. Users post before-and-after photos, and replies often debate whether a result suits the poster's bone structure; one reply to a results post argued that implants would have been the better route [15]. Another poster who was injected to even out a larger side reported new hollowing, thought the jaw looked narrower than they liked, and said they were considering filler if the effect did not wear off [16]. Threads also compare the toxin with chewing-based jaw training, sometimes under the label "chewmaxx" [25].

A recurring view in these threads is that masseter Botox suits wide, square or short lower faces and is a poorer fit for narrow faces, which is a community opinion that none of the cited trials tested. Search-interest data and social-media studies indicate the topic is widely discussed outside forums as well [4][6].

timeline.event: Richard Clark reports cosmetic toxin use for forehead asymmetry, often cited as the first aesthetic use [18].
First reported aesthetic use of toxin for masseter hypertrophy, per Grokipedia [19].
A five-patient ultrasound and EMG study reports a 31 percent reduction in masseter bulk at three months [22].
US FDA approves Botox Cosmetic for glabellar lines [18].
Park and colleagues report ultrasound and CT measurements of lower-face contouring in 45 patients [23].
A 1,021-patient case series concludes toxin can replace surgical masseter resection [21].
FDA adds boxed warnings about distant spread of toxin to botulinum toxin products [18].
Rabbit study reports bone loss at underloaded jaw sites after masseter injection [24].
Allergan begins a Phase 2 trial of Botox for masseter muscle hypertrophy [13].
Phase 2b randomised trial of Botox for masseter prominence starts; a literature review summarises contouring and quality-of-life effects [10][2].
Phase 3 trials for masseter muscle prominence begin [11][12][26][27].
Placebo-controlled CT analysis finds no clinically significant mandibular bone-density change [3].

lore.intro: Masseter Botox is discussed on looksmax.org as a lower-face slimming and hollowing option, with recurring debate about skull shape, asymmetry, jaw structure and alternatives such as implants and chewing exercises [15][16][25].

claims.claim: Masseter Botox slims the lower face and creates hollows.
claims.believers: Posters report a slimmer lower third and new hollowing after treatment [15][16].
claims.experts: Reviews and randomised trials report reduced masseter bulk and lower-face volume versus placebo at day 90 [2][13][10].

claims.claim: It suits wide, square faces more than narrow ones.
claims.believers: Forum commenters say it is meant for wide, short skulls and can leave other faces looking narrow or hollow [16].
claims.experts: Kim and colleagues cautioned that after the masseter shrinks, the cheekbone and jaw angle can look relatively prominent, so anatomy should be assessed [21]; no trial has compared outcomes by skull shape.

claims.claim: It can fix an uneven jaw.
claims.believers: One poster injected the larger side more heavily to even out asymmetry [16].
claims.experts: Trials required matched bilateral prominence, and smile asymmetry occurred in 2.5 percent of patients in one retrospective series [10][20].

claims.claim: The toxin may weaken the jawbone.
claims.believers: Users raise concern that a long-weakened muscle could thin the jaw.
claims.experts: A rabbit study found bone loss at underloaded sites [24]; a placebo-controlled human CT analysis found no clinically significant density change [3]; a retrospective radiograph study found region-specific texture changes [5].

claims.claim: Results are temporary and need repeating.
claims.believers: Posters describe effects wearing off and consider alternatives such as filler or implants [16][15].
claims.experts: Reviews report maximum effect near three months and a duration of six to twelve months, with repeat sessions for long-term results [1].

claims.claim: Chewing-based jaw training and toxin sit at opposite ends of the same goal.
claims.believers: Threads compare chewmaxxing with masseter Botox as routes to a different jaw look [25].
claims.experts: Clinical literature describes bruxism and clenching as drivers of masseter enlargement, which toxin reduces [2][17]; no study compares toxin with chewing exercises for appearance.
